1.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking unto all the people all the words of the Lord their God, then spake Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men, saying unto Jeremiah, Thou speakest falsely: the Lord our God hath not sent thee to say, Go not into Egypt to sojourn there. But Baruch the son of Neriah setteth thee on against us, for to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans. So Johanan and all the captains of the forces obeyed not the voice of the Lord, to dwell in the land of Judah, but took all the remnant of Judah, even men, and women, and children, and the king’s daughters. So they came into the land of Egypt, even to Tahpanhes.

schools.summary: Ellicott works the names and the geography: the Greek's variant for Azariah, its reading of aliens for proud men, and a placing of Tahpanhes on the north-eastern frontier where he thinks the emigrants meant to settle.
Gill and Calvin both defend Baruch as wholly innocent of the charge, and both press that the guilt of the descent was general; they part over whether anything can be known of Azariah.
Clarke supplies the surprise that any of the royal house survived and the tradition of the prophet's death at Tahpanhes; Wesley adds only that the town was then the Egyptian king's residence.
Henry finds the cause under the pretext: it was pride, and only by pride comes contention with God and man.

debates.question: Who is the Azariah who speaks first?

positions.position: Jezaniah, or a brother of his, named first because the scheme was his contrivance.
Possibly two brothers lie behind the two names; here he takes precedence of Johanan as chief spokesman.
Nothing certain can be known of him.
Pride, from which alone comes contention with God and man; the proud unhumbled heart is one of God's most daring enemies.
They had no other colour for rebellion than to deny outright that God had spoken.
The naming of the proud men implies that others, left to themselves, would have followed the prophet.

debates.question: Had the charge against Baruch any colour?

positions.position: None: the prophet would not be led by a younger man who was his own secretary, and Baruch had no interest to serve.
None: it was a fallback, taken up when they could find no reason to say Jeremiah had lied.
Some: a later warning suggests an ambition in Baruch, and he was known to advocate submission.

debates.question: Why had the Chaldeans left the king's daughters behind?

positions.position: They may not have known of them, or thought children of concubines could not inherit, or held females ineligible.
They were daughters by concubines, put somewhere safe against disaster and returning with the other exiles.
The men, women and children named are not the remnant already listed but a further group out of other countries.

debates.question: Where was Tahpanhes, and why did they stop there?

positions.position: At the extremity of Lower Egypt near Heliopolis; they halted to get the king's leave to go further in.
On the north-eastern frontier near Pelusium; here they meant to settle.
The Egyptian king's residence at that time.
A city whose name perished with its wealth, barely found in the heathen writers.

outliers.claim: Records the tradition Jerome reports, that it was at Tahpanhes that the people Jeremiah had watched and prayed and suffered for stoned him to death, and he sealed his mission with his blood.
Notes that the Greek appears to follow a different Hebrew and reads all the aliens where the English has all the proud men.

themes: And it came to pass, that when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking unto all the people all the words of the Lord their God, for which the Lord their God had sent him to them, even all these words,

Then spake Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men, saying unto Jeremiah, Thou speakest falsely: the Lord our God hath not sent thee to say, Go not into Egypt to sojourn there:
But Baruch the son of Neriah setteth thee on against us, for to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they might put us to death, and carry us away captives into Babylon.
So Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces, and all the people, obeyed not the voice of the Lord, to dwell in the land of Judah.
But Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces, took all the remnant of Judah, that were returned from all nations, whither they had been driven, to dwell in the land of Judah;

Even men, and women, and children, and the king’s daughters, and every person that Nebuzar–adan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Jeremiah the prophet, and Baruch the son of Neriah.
So they came into the land of Egypt: for they obeyed not the voice of the Lord: thus came they even to Tahpanhes.

8.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah in Tahpanhes, saying, Take great stones in thine hand, and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah; and say unto them, Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will set his throne upon these stones that I have hid; and he shall spread his royal pavilion over them. And I will kindle a fire in the houses of the gods of Egypt; and he shall burn them, and carry them away captives. He shall break also the images of Beth-shemesh, that is in the land of Egypt.

schools.summary: Ellicott recasts both the brickkiln and the royal pavilion against the English, reading a brick dais and, on one alternative, an executioner's cloth; Keil and Delitzsch supply the temple of the sun at Heliopolis and its obelisks.

Gill works the textual variant of the eleventh verse and ascribes the burning to God though others executed it; Calvin keeps the brickkiln literal, insists a sign is unmeaning without the word, and explains why temples are named at all.

Clarke keeps the destruction practical, the wooden gods burnt and the metal carried off, and takes the images for solid gold; Wesley reads the arraying as the spoils with which the conqueror clothes his army.
Henry makes the place of the prophecy the point: when God's ministers are bound the word of the LORD is not, and Jeremiah went by constraint without losing God's favour.

debates.question: Was Jeremiah's going down to Egypt compulsion or providence?

positions.position: Constraint, not choice, but God did not withdraw his favour and the word of the LORD was not bound.
Force as of chains, and he would sooner have died of famine in Judah; yet God ordered the descent, wanting his herald in Egypt.

debates.question: Is the place a brickkiln or a brick dais?

positions.position: A kiln where bricks were burnt or made, standing near the palace gate.
A brick dais or raised pavement before the entrance, of the kind on which a king sat to give judgment; a brickkiln there would be incongruous.

debates.question: What does arraying himself with Egypt as a shepherd puts on his garment mean?

positions.position: The ease and completeness of the conquest, taken with as little opposition as a man putting on his coat.
The spoils, with which the conqueror clothes his army.

debates.question: Why are the temples of Egypt singled out?

positions.position: Because even the cruellest enemies commonly spare temples, so if sanctity will not preserve these, nothing preserves a house.
Because the change of person is significant: God himself kindles the fire and the Chaldean is only his instrument.
Practically: the wooden gods burnt, the metal carried off, idols and people alike going captive.

debates.question: What are the images of Beth-shemesh?

positions.position: Images of the sun, said to have been of solid gold.
The obelisks of the temple, of which one shaft still stands.
The gods of that city, the chief seat of their worship.

outliers.claim: Records an alternative in which the royal pavilion is not the awning of a throne but the leather sheet spread on the pavement where the condemned knelt for the executioner's stroke, making the king an avenger rather than a monarch in state.

Works the textual variant of the eleventh verse — the written form when it cometh, it shall smite, taken with Kimchi of Nebuchadnezzar's army, against the margin's when he cometh, he shall smite, of the king himself — and concludes that both are to be received.

themes: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah in Tahpanhes, saying,
Take great stones in thine hand, and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah;

And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will set his throne upon these stones that I have hid; and he shall spread his royal pavilion over them.
And when he cometh, he shall smite the land of Egypt, and deliver such as are for death to death; and such as are for captivity to captivity; and such as are for the sword to the sword.

And I will kindle a fire in the houses of the gods of Egypt; and he shall burn them, and carry them away captives: and he shall array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd putteth on his garment; and he shall go forth from thence in peace.
He shall break also the images of Beth–shemesh, that is in the land of Egypt; and the houses of the gods of the Egyptians shall he burn with fire.
